meta.title: Half the Injuries
meta.skill_frame: Argument and evidence: a percentage built on two events.

reader.who: Older students who read at about a fourth-grade level.
reader.why_this_level: Measured FK 5.83, 6.14 and 5.79 on the three parts (102, 107 and 100 words), 5.92 together. A percentage is built on three injuries in two seasons, so the reader has to track how little one runner moves the count.
reader.tone: Adult subject. Plain sentences. The lesson must not make the reader feel small.

source.attribution: Original text drafted for argument_evidence 4.3, band 4.3, sequence 4. No external work.
source.text_status: Drafted for the band, accepted on spot check.
source.survey: A club note that reports a halving of injuries from a change of one injury in a season.
source.avoided: No club name, town, or coach name.

session.difficulty_basis: Two injuries last season and one this season is a fall of half, but a difference of one runner among sixty cannot separate the warm-up from luck.

script_overrides.near_copy_2: Say it in your own words. One sentence is enough.

passage.part_1: A running club sends its members a short note at the end of the season. The note says a new warm-up cut injuries by half. It reports two injuries last season and one this season, and it names the two runners. The club has about sixty members, and nearly the same sixty ran in both seasons. Both numbers come from the coach's notebook, and nobody in the club disputes them. One injury instead of two is a fall of fifty percent, which is how the note puts it. The note asks members to keep doing the warm-up at every practice.
passage.part_2: A fall from two to one is a small change in a small number. Small numbers move for reasons nobody records. One runner who steps off a curb badly can move the total, and so can one who misses a month of practice. Over sixty runners, injuries are rare events. Rare events move around from season to season without any cause at all. A club with two injuries one year might have one the next with no change to anything it does. The note treats a difference of one person as a pattern, and a pattern needs more than two seasons and three injuries to show itself.
passage.part_3: Percentages make small differences sound large. Half of two is one, and one is the smallest change the note could report without reporting nothing at all. The claim might still be true, and the warm-up might help every runner who does it before a run. But two seasons and three injuries cannot show that. The numbers are too small to separate the warm-up from luck. A reader can keep doing the warm-up at every practice, because it costs little to try. The note's proof is still only a change of one person, dressed up as a halving.

items.prompt: What does the club's note say the new warm-up did?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. That it cut injuries by half.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The note says the new warm-up cut injuries by half.
tutor_only.tell: The note says the warm-up cut injuries by half.
help: The sentence about the warm-up carries the claim.
It names the size of the fall.
tutor_only.core_idea: The new warm-up cut injuries by half.
accept_ideas: cut injuries by half
halved the injuries
fewer injuries by half
the warm-up halved the injury count
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the note claims the warm-up is faster
if_they_say.ask: The note is about injuries. What did the warm-up do to them?

items.prompt: What counts does the note give for the two seasons?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Two injuries last season and one this season.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The note reports two injuries last season and one this season.
tutor_only.tell: Two injuries last season and one this season.
help: The sentence with the two counts holds both numbers.
It puts one beside each season.
tutor_only.core_idea: Two injuries last season and one this season.
accept_ideas: two last season and one this season
two, then one
two injuries then one injury
two last year and one this year
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student gives both numbers the same value
if_they_say.ask: The note prints one count for each season. What are the two numbers?

items.prompt: Why could a change from two injuries to one come from chance?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. Injuries are rare here, so a single runner raises or lowers the total.
tutor_only.correct_reason: Over sixty runners injuries are rare events, and one runner who steps badly or misses a month moves the total.
tutor_only.tell: Injuries are rare among sixty runners, so one bad step moves the count.
help: The sentences about rare events carry the answer.
They name one runner as enough to change the count.
tutor_only.core_idea: Because injuries among sixty runners are rare, so one runner can move the count by itself.
accept_ideas: one runner can move the count
injuries are rare at this club
rare events move around from season to season
a single bad step changes the total
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says the club got luckier weather
if_they_say.ask: The club counted three injuries in two seasons. What does one runner weigh in that count?

items.prompt: A reader says the note proves the warm-up cut injuries. Is that shown?

tutor_only.confirm: No. One injury fewer is too small a change to separate the warm-up from luck.
tutor_only.correct_reason: A fall from two to one moves the whole percentage, so the number is too small to show what caused the difference.
tutor_only.tell: No. With counts this small, one lucky season looks the same as a warm-up that works.
help: The sentences about rare events and two seasons carry the answer.
They show how little one injury means here.
tutor_only.core_idea: No, because a change of one injury is too small to separate the warm-up from luck.
accept_ideas: no, one injury is too small a change
no, two seasons cannot show it
no, the numbers are too small
no, luck could explain one injury
not_required: how many members the club has
tutor_only.normalize: Ignore case, punctuation, and minor spelling. Accept a meaning-preserving paraphrase.

if_they_say.when: the student says fifty percent is a large fall, so the warm-up works
if_they_say.ask: Half of two is one. How much does one runner move a club of sixty?

items.prompt: What would the club need to show the warm-up works?

tutor_only.confirm: Right. More seasons or more runners, so the counts are large enough to compare.
tutor_only.correct_reason: The club would need enough injuries over enough seasons for the counts to separate the warm-up from luck.
tutor_only.tell: More seasons and more injuries, so the counts can show a real difference.
help: The sentences about sixty runners and two seasons name the shortage.
They show what a pattern would need.
tutor_only.core_idea: More seasons or more runners, so the counts are large enough to compare.
accept_ideas: more seasons of data
a much larger group of runners
enough injuries to compare
many more seasons than two

if_they_say.when: the student says the club should count the same two seasons again
if_they_say.ask: Two seasons gave three injuries. Would a fourth season settle it? What has to grow?
